title: Give, and it will be given (Luke 6:27–38)
hook: good measure, pressed down, shaken together, running over

segments.voice: Yesterday, the plain, four blessings and four woes. Your line was blessed are you poor. Whose name did you learn, and how did they look at you? Day five hundred twenty-four.

At a grain market, you hold out your measure, a basket or a jar, and the seller fills it. A stingy seller fills it loosely, full of air pockets, and levels it off flat. A generous one does something else. He pours the grain in, then presses it down with his hand. Shakes the container so the grain settles. Pours in more. Presses again. Keeps going until it's heaped up and spilling over the sides, and you have to hold out the fold of your robe to catch the rest. That's the picture Jesus ends this teaching with. But first, he says some very hard things.

Still on the level place, Jesus says, in the King James words: "Love your enemies, do good to them which hate you, Bless them that curse you, and pray for them which despitefully use you." Turn the other cheek. Give to everyone who asks. Lend, hoping for nothing back. And the line now called the Golden Rule: "as ye would that men should do to you, do ye also to them likewise." Then the center of it all: "Be ye therefore merciful, as your Father also is merciful." Mercy is the measure. And then the picture from the market: "Give, and it shall be given unto you; good measure, pressed down, and shaken together, and running over, shall men give into your bosom." Bosom here isn't your chest. The Greek word, kolpos, can mean the lap or the fold of a robe, which could hold grain like a pouch. So the image is a lap overflowing. And then the hinge: "For with the same measure that ye mete withal it shall be measured to you again." Mete means to measure out. Whatever size of basket you use on others is the basket that comes back to you. This isn't a get-rich promise. A few lines earlier, Jesus has told people to lend, hoping for nothing again. In its place, the measure is about mercy: judge not, condemn not, forgive, give, and the same measure comes back. The basket you hold out to others is the basket you're handed. Running over.
screen: then, large: `GIVE, AND IT SHALL BE GIVEN UNTO YOU.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: give with a heaped measure. Settle, and breathe. Picture your hands as the seller's hands at the market, holding a basket of grain. Now think of someone you could give to today. It might be money, but it might be time, praise, patience, attention, a long phone call. Notice your first instinct about how much: level it off, just enough. Now picture pressing it down. Shaking it together. Adding a bit more. What would the heaped version look like? A longer visit. A bigger tip. A real compliment instead of a quick one. Decide on the generous version. If you pray, you can ask for open hands. If you don't, simply picture the basket overflowing. The bell holds the time.
Give. Jesus' teaching on the plain: be merciful, give without counting, and what you give comes back pressed down, shaken together and running over.
Your line: running over. Give the heaped version of whatever you planned to give today, and watch what spills back. Day five hundred twenty-four.

howItsDone: Christians often read Luke 6:38 as a call to generous giving, alongside the Golden Rule in Luke 6:31.

fork.reveal: Jesus' picture is the heaped measure, pressed and shaken until it spills into the lap. the measure you use is the one that comes back.

original.note: Greek: lap, bosom, the fold of a garment. where the overflowing measure is poured.

trapdoor: what you thought: give, and you'll get rich.
what it means: in a teaching about mercy and lending without return, Jesus says generosity shapes the life you get back.
what a scholar hears: the overflowing measure is poured into the kolpos, a word that can mean the lap or the fold of a garment.
recall: friend of God, or loved by God
